data.title: Pityriasis rosea — viva
data.summary: Papulosquamous & erythroderma · 9 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Pityriasis rosea** (Papulosquamous & erythroderma)_

**Q1. Define pityriasis rosea (PR).**
- Acute, self-limiting papulosquamous eruption with a herald patch followed by a secondary eruption of oval scaly patches along skin cleavage lines, usually in adolescents and young adults (10–35 y); resolves in 6–8 weeks

**Q2. Aetiology.**
- Reactivation of human herpesvirus 7 (and HHV-6) — supported by DNA/mRNA in lesions, clustering, prodrome, seasonal pattern (spring/autumn), rare recurrence
- PR-like drug eruptions: ACE inhibitors (captopril), gold, metronidazole, isotretinoin, terbinafine, NSAIDs, imatinib, beta-blockers, vaccines (influenza, BCG, COVID-19)

**Q3. Describe the clinical course.**
- Prodrome in some (malaise, sore throat, headache)
- Herald patch (mother patch) in ~80%: single larger (2–10 cm) oval salmon-pink patch with a peripheral collarette of fine scale (scale attached at the edge, free towards centre) on trunk
- 1–2 weeks later: crops of smaller similar oval patches with long axis along Langer's lines — 'Christmas tree' pattern on back, 'V' on chest; mostly trunk and proximal limbs (bathing suit distribution); face, palms spared
- Itch mild–moderate; resolves in 6–8 weeks (up to 12), may leave hypo/hyperpigmentation in dark skin

**Q4. Name the atypical variants.**
- Inverse PR (flexures, face, distal limbs — commoner in children and dark skin)
- Papular (common in Indian/African children), vesicular, urticarial, purpuric/haemorrhagic, pustular, erythema multiforme-like, giant (pityriasis rosea gigantea of Darier), localised/unilateral, oral lesions
- Herald patch only, multiple herald patches, relapsing PR, persistent PR (>12 weeks)

**Q5. Why is PR in pregnancy important?**
- PR in the first 15 weeks of pregnancy is associated with miscarriage/premature delivery (HHV-6/7 reactivation) — consider acyclovir and obstetric follow-up

**Q6. Differential diagnosis.**
- Secondary syphilis (palms/soles, mucosa, lymphadenopathy, no herald patch — always do VDRL in sexually active adults with atypical PR)
- Tinea corporis (herald patch confusion — KOH), guttate psoriasis, nummular eczema, pityriasis versicolor, PR-like drug eruption, pityriasis lichenoides chronica, seborrhoeic dermatitis, MF (persistent), viral exanthems

**Q7. Histopathology.**
- Non-specific subacute spongiotic dermatitis with focal mounds of parakeratosis, extravasated RBCs in papillary dermis, superficial perivascular lymphocytes, dyskeratotic cells

**Q8. Treatment.**
- Reassurance — self-limiting; emollients, calamine, mild topical steroids, oral antihistamines for itch
- Acyclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days (or 400 mg TDS) early in extensive/symptomatic disease — shortens course in some trials
- Erythromycin (older evidence, inconsistent)
- NB-UVB/sunlight for extensive itchy cases (may increase post-inflammatory pigmentation)

**Q9. What is the collarette scale?**
- Fine scale attached at the periphery with free edge pointing inwards — seen in PR, also in some tinea, healing bullous impetigo, AGEP desquamation

## Quick spotter facts
- Herald patch + Christmas-tree pattern — pityriasis rosea
- Always exclude secondary syphilis (VDRL)
- HHV-6/7

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Pityriasis rosea). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
